title: NSA sliding-window KV compression
formula: out[i,n,:] = sum_{j<L} input[win_start[i]+j, n, :] * weight[j, n], accumulated in fp32 in the upstream ReduceBlock fold order and rounded once to the storage dtype with ties away from zero; a batch of sequence length S contributes floor((S-L)/d)+1 whole windows when S >= L and none otherwise; fp16 or bf16 [T,N,D] input with [L,N] weight and an int32 [Tc] table of window starts -> [Tc,N,D] output
study_for: Two rounding decisions that a tolerance would have hidden, and how each was caught. The single narrowing cast breaks ties AWAY FROM ZERO (AscendC CAST_ROUND, `RoundMode.AWAY_FROM_ZERO`), where `torch.Tensor.to` breaks them to even -- 14 of 200000 random fp16 values disagree, every one an exact tie. And fp32 addition is not associative, so the ORDER of the L-term sum is observable too: grep `fold_plan` in kernel.py and `reduction_order` in reference.py for the upstream ReduceBlock order, which folds the non-power-of-two remainder onto the front and then halves the stride. Both are stated twice, once per file, and the demo's exact comparison is what holds them together.

What an upstream oracle is worth. The rounding mode was recovered by reading sources; the reduction order was not. Running the real vendor operator on an A2 card (`torch_npu.npu_nsa_compress`) against this reference disagreed on 4 of 9216 elements in ut_a1_fp16 -- and recomputing those four windows three ways showed all four matching the tree and none matching a serial sum. Nothing below hardware would have found it: sim, pipesim and the card all agreed with the wrong reference, because the kernel had the same wrong order.

Why the fold is a loop over `(stride, count)` and not the expression tree it is equivalent to. A depth-first walk of the tree needs only log2(L) live registers and no staging buffer, and it emits correctly -- then bisheng spills it, because the walk unrolls into straight-line code: measured at L = 32, 35 vector slots and 8992 bytes against a 6144-byte VF stack. Staging the products in UB and folding them with small device loops keeps the emitted body near 120 lines for every L. A static Python container is what makes the strides compile-time without any device division, which would otherwise have pulled in the integer-cast supplement.

A hazard the simulator does not model. The folds read what the products loop wrote and each fold reads the one before it, and a UB store inside a `@vf` is not visible to a later load without `vf_barrier(VfPipe.STORE, VfPipe.LOAD)`. Without those barriers sim and pipesim both stayed green on every case while the card returned every case wrong. Grep `vf_barrier`: one after the staging loop, one after each fold.

Sizing the backing a whole-register access needs, which is not one rule. M10-088 makes a LANES-wide footprint real however few columns are live, so `_geometry` gives the two read-only tiles spare ROWS -- an overrunning read lands in the next row, which is written later or is spare -- and gives the staged products a LANES-aligned row PITCH instead, because the folds read and write them in place and an overrunning store would clobber a row that is still live. The first shape is what the emit gate forces: a wider tile with a narrower transfer into it is refused as `dma.gm_to_ub.pad: a partial transfer into a tile window stacks two validshapes`, which is also why `head_tile` returns a DIVISOR of N so every group is the same constant width.

How a data-dependent output length reaches a backend that specialises per scalar valuation. The upstream output row count is computed from the VALUES of an int64 prefix sum (its infershape reads them). Grep `window_starts` in reference.py: the host expands that into one absolute row index per output token and the device takes an int32 table, so no int64 reaches the card. The justification is a boundary rather than convenience -- the upstream's own tiling already reads actSeqLen to derive kvStartTokenIdx and PerCoreStartOutputOffset. `start.GetValueFrom(...)` then feeds only an address: every tile dimension stays a compile-time integer, which is the line RFC-0013 draws and attention.a5_pfa_hif8_task_metadata records the other side of.

Where the time went, measured, and what each measurement changed. One Ascend950PR card, the board launcher's profiler (device-side Task Duration, not host wall time -- the harness round trip is ~7.6 s per launch and identical for a 0.01 MB case and a 2.9 MB one), on a 302 MB input because this part's L2 holds 112 MiB and every demo shape fits in it several times over. block_dim 8 -> 28 was 3.48x; fusing the first reduction fold into the products loop was 1.10x and halved the staged tile; double-buffering the window and the output row was another 1.92x (1034 -> 535 us at L == stride). The re-read of an overlapped window, which looked like the obvious target, measured free and was never written: the L = 2*stride shape requests 1.91x the bytes for 1.24x the time at identical UNIQUE traffic, because the re-read rows are still in L2. The per-pipe ratios are what said which to do: before double buffering nothing exceeded 0.53, so it was dependency-bound rather than pipe-bound; after, `aiv_mte2` 0.955 leads at L == stride and `aiv_vec` 0.986 leads at L = 2*stride, which is the crossover the timing already implied.

Two defects the simulator cannot see, and the case each one needed. (1) The weight splat writes one whole register per head, which covers a head of 64 columns or fewer by overrunning into the next -- and covers only the first 64 columns of a wider one. Every case here had D <= 64 except the D = 256 one, and that shape routes to the sub-head group, so the wide whole-head path had no case at all: reaching a constraint's extreme value is not the same as reaching the code path that value takes. `wide_head_multi_chunk` is the case that does. (2) The pipeline's prefetch, left unguarded, wrote the next window into `xa` after the last pair of a column group had already consumed it -- a write with no reader, whose only successor is the next group's prologue write to the same tile. On the card the stale one won and the first output row of every group after the first came out of the previous group's columns. sim, pipesim, PyPTO-Pro and CCE all called it correct, and CCE failing the same way is what proved it was ours; `many_head_groups` is the only case with a second group for the first one's epilogue to race.
do_not_copy_when: You need the overlapped regime to be traffic-optimal on a part with a smaller L2, or with a stride so much smaller than the window that the halo no longer fits. On this part it measured free (see the last study_for entry), so the halo scheme -- a core owning a contiguous run of output tokens and loading it once with an L-stride halo -- was deliberately not written. That is a measured choice, not an unexamined limit, and the measurement is what you would have to redo rather than the reasoning.

Your head count is prime and your head is wide. `column_tile` prefers the widest DIVISOR of N whose group fits, then falls back to a slice of one head, so the geometry is always uniform and always a compile-time constant -- a ragged last group would need the partial transfer into a wider tile that the emit gate refuses. The cost lands on a shape like N = 7 with a head too wide to pair up: one head per group, one transfer per head per token. Correct, and more transfers than a ragged split would need.

You want the upstream ABI. This takes [T, N*D] and [1, L*N] views plus a host-built int32 window table; it does not take layout strings, an int64 actSeqLen, actSeqLenType, or anything but the TND layout the upstream itself restricts to.

You want a number for a different part, a different launch width or a different backend. Everything above is one card, PyPTO-Pro, the block_dim each case names -- and a `block_dim` tuned for one card is not tuned for another, with nothing here to notice that for you. CCE appears only as a control that adjudicates a failure; it is not what this demo delivers.
